title: Global vs Local Ancestry Modeling
subtitle: When locus-specific ancestry changes the story, and when it does not
learningObjectives: Differentiate global ancestry adjustment from local ancestry-informed modeling.
Predict that local ancestry buys power only when the effect differs between backgrounds.
Explain why the global scan wins when the effect is similar, even if allele frequencies differ.

prediction.question: The tag SNP has opposite effects on African- and European-ancestry haplotypes (+0.12 and -0.08) in a 15,000-person admixed study. Which is the simplest analysis that detects it at p < 0.05?

options.label: Adding local ancestry as a covariate

controls.label: African local ancestry at this locus (%)

presets.label: Opposite effects
presets.description: Opposite LD phase on African and European haplotypes; the pooled estimate cancels and only the interaction model sees the locus.

presets.label: Same effect, different frequency
presets.description: The same +0.08 effect on both backgrounds although the allele frequency differs (0.11 African vs 0.34 European); the plain scan wins, because local ancestry has nothing to add and the extra parameters cost power.

presets.label: One background only
presets.description: An effect carried on African-ancestry haplotypes alone; the backgrounds differ, so local ancestry helps.

presets.label: Too small to tell
presets.description: The same opposing effects in a study a third of the size; no model sees the locus.

simulatedEffects.mechanism: Participant-set: LD phase with the causal allele on African haplotypes
Participant-set: opposite LD phase on European haplotypes at the default setting
Fixed: mixed haplotype background; effect largely cancels

interpretation.prompt: Does modelling local ancestry at this locus buy power, cost power, or neither?
interpretation.whatChanged: With opposing effects the standard scan reports nothing at this locus: the pooled estimate averages the two directions to near zero. Adding local ancestry as a covariate does not rescue it, because the problem is effect modification rather than confounding. Only the interaction model, which fits one slope per background and combines them, separates the backgrounds. Set both effects the same and the verdict reverses: the plain scan wins even though the allele frequency differs (0.11 vs 0.34), because local ancestry has nothing to add and the interaction model pays for its extra parameters in degrees of freedom.
interpretation.whyItMatters: Local-ancestry modelling is stratify-then-combine (Tractor), the same choice as modules 1 and 2 made at one locus. It buys power only when the effect genuinely differs between ancestry backgrounds; when the effect is similar, global ancestry adjustment is the better analysis even if the allele frequency is not. There is no one right way, and a null from the wrong model is not the same as no biology.
interpretation.facilitatorNote: Collect the prediction before anyone touches a control, then project the room's split. The middle option is the intuitive one and it is wrong: local ancestry as a covariate does almost nothing here, because the backgrounds disagree rather than confound. The interaction model is the Tractor idea from the framing slides: stratify the genotype by local ancestry, estimate one effect per background, then combine, which is module 1's stratified analysis and module 2's meta-analysis done at a single locus. Then send them to the presets. 'Same effect, different frequency' is the one that surprises people who have just learned to reach for the interaction model: the frequencies differ three-fold, the effects agree, and the plain scan wins. Say the take-home out loud: local ancestry improves power only when the effect differs between populations; when it is similar, global ancestry is better even with different allele frequencies; there is no one right way. Watch the 'best here' line on the detection panel change hands as they move the sliders. Module 4 is the cost side of this trade-off at small sample sizes.

Which setting would make you distrust a published pooled estimate at this locus?
Would you choose the model before seeing the data, and what would you need to know to choose?

alleleFrequencies.note: MTHFR C677T. Common in every continental group but at materially different frequencies, so a pooled analysis is well powered while still averaging over groups.

realInputs.ancestryDistribution: All of Us Research Program, genomic data release v7 (~245,000 short-read whole genomes); ancestry proportions rounded to whole percent.

syntheticInputs: Background-specific effect sizes are set by the participant over -0.12 to 0.12 phenotype SD per allele (default +0.12 African, -0.08 European); they are not published MTHFR effect estimates.
The Admixed American background is fixed at +0.03 phenotype SD per allele, and the non-African local ancestry share keeps a 0.31:0.17 European-to-Admixed American ratio.
Local ancestry at the locus (20-80% African) and the 180 kb LD decay constant are illustrative.
assumptions: Additive dosage model, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, continuous phenotype standardised to unit variance.
Effects are per local-ancestry background: a tag SNP in opposite LD phase with an untyped causal variant carries opposite signs on different ancestral haplotypes.
Global-PC model: slope = sum(p_g f_g b_g) / sum(p_g f_g), the marginal regression. Global principal components carry no locus-specific ancestry information, so they leave this slope unchanged.

Local-ancestry-covariate model: slope = sum(p_g f_g (1-f_g) b_g) / sum(p_g f_g (1-f_g)), the within-background slope weighted by genotype variance; its standard error subtracts the genotype variance that ancestry explains.

Local-ancestry-interaction model: one slope per background, with standard errors from the background's sample size and allele frequency, tested jointly on three degrees of freedom. This is the local-ancestry-deconvolved (Tractor-style) regression, reduced to a single locus.
Covariate counts: 12 (age, sex, ten PCs), 13 (plus local-ancestry dosage), and 16 (plus per-background genotype terms); each absorbs k/n of the genotype variance by chance.
Local ancestry is constant across the displayed window: admixture tracts from recent admixture span megabases, not the 400 kb shown here.
Tag markers carry the signal attenuated by exp(-distance / 180 kb).
Two-sided Wald tests at alpha = 0.05; the regional threshold line is Bonferroni-corrected for the markers in the displayed window.
provenance.derived: Standard errors, p-values, power, meta-analysis summaries, and heterogeneity statistics are computed from the inputs above by analysis/genetics.py; none are hand-entered.
